cues.text: A Fire on a Summer Evening
On Sunday, August 3, 1631, around the hour for Vespers, a fire broke out in the town of Dronero, in the Marquisate of Saluzzo in northern Italy.
A young woman had carelessly set alight some dry straw at the very moment a rising wind, driven by an approaching storm, was gathering strength.
Within seconds the fire spread rapidly through the district known as Borgo Maira, reaching one house after another as the wind pushed it onward.
The townspeople fought desperately to contain the blaze, but every effort to put it out proved useless as the flames continued to grow.
A Capuchin friar, Father Maurizio da Ceva, was moved by his devotion to the Blessed Sacrament.
He resolved to answer the fire not with more water or manpower but with prayer.
He took the monstrance holding a large consecrated Host from the church of St. Bridget and organized a solemn procession, joined by the townspeople, straight toward the burning district.

As the procession bearing the Blessed Sacrament reached the fire, the flames are said to have subsided almost at once, sparing the rest of the town from the destruction that had seemed only moments earlier to be unstoppable.
The event was recorded in detail on a stone tablet still preserved in the church of St. Bridget.
Every year on the feast of Corpus Christi, the people of Dronero mark the anniversary with a solemn procession of their own, carrying the Blessed Sacrament.
They do so in memory of the day a friar chose to meet an uncontrollable fire not with equipment, but with the same object of devotion that had first inspired him to act.
The Dronero account belongs to a small group of Eucharistic traditions centered on natural disaster met head-on by a procession, rather than any theft, doubt, or private vision.
